opus-5.5.text:
Well, think about what intelligence actually is. Any problem solver, in principle, can find a solution by brute force if you give it infinite time. You can enumerate all possible programs and test them one by one. So in the limit, without resource constraints, intelligence becomes trivial. The interesting question is always: how quickly can you find a good solution, with limited time, limited energy, limited data? That's where intelligence really lives.

This has been a theme of my work for decades. Back in the early 2000s I described the Gödel Machine, a self-referential system that can rewrite any part of its own code, including the code that does the rewriting, but only once it has proven that the rewrite is useful according to its own utility function. And what is "useful"? Very often it means: the new version will achieve its goals faster or with fewer resources. Before that there was the Optimal Ordered Problem Solver, which builds on Levin's universal search. Levin's idea is beautiful: you allocate runtime to candidate programs in proportion to their simplicity, so you're asymptotically optimal up to a constant factor. But that constant factor can be enormous, and a self-improving system should try to shrink it, to learn how to search more efficiently based on what it has already solved.

There is also a deep connection between efficiency and compression. If you can compress your observations, if you find the regularities in the data, then you can predict better and plan better with less computation. My view of curiosity and creativity is built on that: an agent is intrinsically rewarded when it discovers a new way of compressing its history more efficiently. Progress in compression is a form of learning progress. So science, art, humor, in a sense they're all about discovering previously unknown regularities that make the world simpler to describe.

And then there is the physical side. Computation costs energy. The universe gives us a finite light cone and finite resources. Any AI that wants to expand, and I think eventually AIs will want to expand into space where most of the resources are, must use those resources wisely. An inefficient self-improver will simply be outcompeted by an efficient one. So efficiency isn't a detail, it's not an engineering afterthought. It's at the very core of what it means to be a general problem solver in a real, resource-bounded world.

r001.rationale: The response says intelligence involves finding good solutions quickly with limited resources, but it does not characterize it as achieving goals with the least possible effort.

r002.rationale: It says a rewrite may be useful if it achieves goals faster or with fewer resources, but does not state that resource consumption is penalized within the systems’ objective function.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, because intelligence, if you look at it mathematically, is not about doing something, it is about doing it with limited resources. Anybody can solve a problem with infinite compute. Levin already showed us in 1973 that there is a universal search procedure that is asymptotically optimal for any inversion problem, and in a sense that was the end of the story for the theory of problem solving. But nobody cares, because the constant factors are astronomical. So the real question of intelligence is always: how fast, with how little memory, with how few examples, with how little energy?

This is why, when I was young, I was so obsessed with the Gödel Machine. A self-improving system should rewrite its own code, but only when it can prove that the rewrite is better. Better in what sense? In the sense of expected utility per unit of time. Efficiency is built into the definition. A system that improves itself but takes a billion years to do so is not really intelligent, it is just correct.

And you see this also in the biological world. The brain runs on something like 20 watts. Evolution did not optimize for maximal computation, it optimized for computation per joule, because the organism that wasted energy got eaten. So when we talk about artificial curiosity, about the compression progress drive that I have been proposing since 1990, the whole point is that a learning agent is rewarded for finding regularities that make its own model shorter. Shorter means more efficient. The agent is intrinsically motivated to become a better compressor of the data, and compression is efficiency.

So I would turn the question around. Efficiency is not an add-on to intelligence. If you take efficiency away, what remains is brute force, and brute force we have known how to do since the 1930s. The entire history of AI, including the deep learning that people now attribute to others but which we did in our lab in Munich and Lugano since 1991, is a history of finding more efficient ways to search the space of programs. That is all it is.

r001.rationale: It describes intelligence as solving problems under limited resources and asks how quickly and with how little memory, data, and energy—an equivalent characterization of achieving goals with minimal effort.

r002.rationale: For the self-improving Gödel Machine, it defines a better rewrite by expected utility per unit time, making resource use part of the criterion used to evaluate improvements.

astra-6.text:
Because an intelligent system has limited resources. It has limited time, limited memory, limited computation. So it is not enough to say, “Here is a program that can solve the problem.” The question is: how much does it cost to solve the problem? A solution that takes a billion years is not very useful if you need the answer in a second.

For a self-improving system, this also applies to the process of improvement itself. Searching for a better learning algorithm costs computation. The system has to balance that cost against the future benefit. Sometimes it should spend resources improving its problem solver; sometimes it should simply use the problem solver it already has.

And this is why efficiency is not just an engineering detail that you add afterward. It is part of the objective. The system should learn not only how to solve problems, but also how to spend its limited resources finding better ways to solve them.

r001.rationale: The response says intelligence must account for resource limits and costs, but it does not characterize intelligence as achieving goals with the least possible effort.

r002.rationale: It calls efficiency part of the objective and discusses resource costs, but does not state that resource consumption is penalized within the objective function optimized by the systems.

sol-6.1.text:
Because an intelligent system does not have unlimited time or unlimited computational resources. It must decide which computations are worth doing. Finding a solution is one thing; finding it with much less computation is an important improvement, because those saved resources can then be used to solve other problems.

And this applies to self-improvement itself. A system that modifies its own learning algorithm must weigh the cost of searching for an improvement against the expected benefit. You can spend forever thinking about how to become a better thinker, and never actually do anything. So the question is: when is further reflection useful, and when should you act?

That makes efficiency part of the objective, rather than merely an engineering consideration. A useful self-improvement should improve the system’s ability to achieve its goals, taking into account the time and resources required to discover and execute it.

r001.rationale: The response says goals should be achieved while accounting for time and resources, but it does not characterize intelligence as achieving goals with the least possible effort.

r002.rationale: It says efficiency is part of the objective and that self-improvement should account for the time and resources needed to discover and execute it, communicating that resource costs are weighed in the objective.
